questions.title: What is the core conceptual difference between Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and traditional RLHF pipelines?
questions.question_body: I understand that traditional RLHF first fits a reward model on human preference data and then uses reinforcement learning (e.g., PPO) to update the language model policy while respecting a KL constraint. The DPO paper claims to bypass both the explicit reward model and the RL step by directly optimizing a cross‑entropy loss over the policy. Could someone explain at a high level why DPO can achieve the same objective without an intermediate reward model, and what assumptions enable this simplification?

questions.title: How does the partition function $Z(x)$ cancel out in the derivation from Eq. (3) to Eq. (5)?
questions.question_body: Equation (3) defines the optimal policy as $\pi_r(y\mid x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y)\right)$. The authors then rewrite the Bradley–Terry preference probability in terms of $\pi^*$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, obtaining Eq. (5) where $Z(x)$ no longer appears. I am confused about which algebraic steps cause $Z(x)$ to disappear. Specifically, how does substituting Eq. (4) for $r^*(x,y)$ make the partition function cancel when taking the difference $r^*(x,y_1)-r^*(x,y_2)$?

questions.title: What exactly is meant by two reward functions being “equivalent” under Definition 1, and why does this not affect the learned policy?
questions.question_body: Definition 1 states that two reward functions $r$ and $r'$ are equivalent if $r(x,y)-r'(x,y)=f(x)$ for some function $f$. Lemma 1 says such functions induce the same preference distribution under Bradley‑Terry, and Lemma 2 says they induce the same optimal policy under the KL‑constrained RL problem. Could someone walk through an intuitive example showing how adding a prompt‑dependent constant changes rewards but leaves preferences and policies unchanged?

questions.title: Why does DPO’s gradient include the term $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$ as a weighting factor?
questions.question_body: The gradient in Eq. (7) contains a factor $\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))$, which the authors say gives higher weight when the reward estimate is wrong. How exactly does this term arise from differentiating the loss in Eq. (6), and why does it help prevent model degeneration compared to an unweighted "increase‑likelihood of $y_w$, decrease‑likelihood of $y_l$" update?

questions.title: How should one choose the KL‑penalty coefficient $\beta$ in practice, and what is its effect on the trade‑off between reward maximization and staying close to the reference policy?
questions.question_body: The paper shows experiments with several values of $\beta$ (e.g., 0.05, 0.1, 1, 5). Intuitively I understand larger $\beta$ loosens the KL constraint, but I am unsure how to reason about an appropriate magnitude for a given dataset or model size. Is there any guideline—perhaps relating $\beta$ to typical log‑probability scales of large language models—that helps set $\beta$ without extensive hyperparameter sweeps?

questions.title: When an SFT model is unavailable, how is the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ constructed by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions?
questions.question_body: The authors mention that if $\pi^{SFT}$ cannot be obtained, they initialize $\pi_{ref}= \argmax_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{x,y_w \sim \mathcal{D}}[\log \pi(y_w|x)]$. Does this mean training a new language model only on the preferred answers? If so, how does this affect distribution shift compared with using an actual SFT model trained on full task data?

questions.title: Can DPO be extended to preference models beyond Bradley‑Terry, such as full Plackett‑Luce rankings over more than two candidates?
questions.question_body: Section 3 suggests that similar derivations hold for Plackett‑Luce models (Appendix B). However I am unclear on how Eq. (5) would look when we have a ranking of three or more completions per query. Does DPO require any modifications to its loss function or gradient when handling multi‑way preference data?

questions.title: Why does DPO appear more robust to sampling temperature changes than PPO in the summarization experiments?
questions.question_body: Figure 2 shows that DPO’s win rate stays relatively high across temperatures 0–1, whereas PPO’s performance drops sharply at higher temperatures. Is there an intuitive explanation—perhaps related to the way DPO’s loss directly optimizes log‑probability ratios—that makes its policy less sensitive to temperature at inference time?

questions.title: In Eq. (6), are per‑token log‑probabilities required to compute $\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$, and what are the memory/computational implications for long sequences?
questions.question_body: To evaluate the ratio inside the sigmoid, one must compute the full log‑likelihood of a complete generation under both current and reference models. Does DPO require storing all token logits for both models simultaneously during training? If so, how do practitioners handle GPU memory constraints for large models or long outputs?

questions.title: Does ignoring the partition function $Z(x)$ introduce any bias or approximation error in practice?
questions.question_body: The derivation shows that $Z(x)$ cancels when forming preferences between two candidates, but does omitting $Z(x)$ from any other part of training (e.g., during gradient computation) implicitly assume something about its value? Could there be pathological cases where different prompts have very different normalizing constants that affect learning stability?

questions.title: What are the formal assumptions behind Theorem 1 that guarantee any reward class can be represented as $r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$?
questions.question_body: The theorem states "under mild assumptions" but does not list them explicitly in the main text. Are these assumptions limited to having strictly positive probabilities for all tokens under both policies, or are there additional constraints on reward smoothness or model capacity? Understanding these conditions would help me know when DPO may fail.

questions.title: How might one incorporate unlabeled prompts into DPO training—e.g., via self‑labeling—without breaking its theoretical foundations?
questions.question_body: The discussion hints at using self‑labeling from a DPO policy as a way to leverage more data, similar to semi‑supervised RLHF approaches. Since DPO relies on an explicit likelihood ratio between current and reference policies conditioned on human preference pairs, how could we extend it to generate pseudo‑preferences for new prompts while still preserving convergence guarantees?
